narrative.headline: Gukesh's long think produces a novelty, Bd7
narrative.text: Gukesh spent 15 minutes 32 seconds on 13...Bd7, the move that took the game out of known theory, and the engine still rates it a good move. The engine's top choice was the quiet pawn move h5, with f6 and a5 close behind, and it counted at least 5 good moves, so Gukesh had plenty of reasonable options. One likely reason for the long think is that all three engine favourites were pawn moves that commit the pawn structure, while Bd7 is a flexible bishop move that keeps the structure intact. Gukesh was also probably working things out at the board for the first time, since this was a novelty played right after Sindarov's quick 13.Ne4. The think was Gukesh's second-longest of the game, following 12 and a half minutes on 12...Be7. Gukesh started the move nearly 20 minutes behind on the clock, and afterwards had 1h 19m left against Sindarov's 1h 54m.

likely_reasons.reason: Gukesh left known theory with this move, so Gukesh probably had to work out the position alone.
The engine's top options were all pawn moves that commit the structure, so Gukesh may have spent time weighing them against a flexible bishop move.
With at least 5 good moves and very low difficulty, the time probably went into choosing among many reasonable options rather than avoiding a single trap.

narrative.headline: Gukesh spends 36 minutes finding the engine's choice
narrative.text: Gukesh played 17...Bb4, which is exactly the engine's top move, and the engine rates the position as roughly balanced at -0.33 for Gukesh. The decision cost 36 minutes and 14 seconds, Gukesh's longest think of the game, dropping the clock from 1h 04m to 28m 40s against Sindarov's 1h 18m. One likely reason is that there were at least 5 good moves and the top choices were almost equal: the engine had f5 and Bc8 only a hair behind Bb4. Those options are different in kind, because f5 commits the pawn structure and leads to trades, while Bb4 keeps things flexible with no captures early in the line. Sindarov's previous move 17.b3 changed the pawn structure and created tension, which may have prompted a fresh reassessment. Gukesh had also left known theory with 13...Bd7 only four moves earlier and had already spent long thinks on 12...Be7 and 13...Bd7, so Gukesh was probably working things out alone at the board.

likely_reasons.reason: Several good moves with nearly identical evaluations but very different characters probably made choosing between them hard.
Sindarov's 17.b3 changed the pawn structure and created tension, which may have required a new assessment.
Gukesh had left theory just four moves earlier and was likely calculating without preparation, as the earlier long thinks also suggest.

narrative.headline: Sindarov spends time choosing a pawn commitment
narrative.text: Sindarov played 21.g4 after 8 minutes 36 seconds, the engine's second choice, and it was classed as a good move. The engine preferred the knight retreat Ne1, which leads to rook trades, and the evaluation slipped from +0.32 to about -0.04, a level position. There were 3 good moves on the table, each quite different: a knight retreat, a king move with Kh2, and the pawn push g4, which permanently commits the pawn structure. That kind of irreversible choice probably deserved some care, even though Gukesh had answered quickly with 20...Rg8 in just 11 seconds. The game had been out of known theory for seven moves since Gukesh's 13...Bd7, and Sindarov had already invested long thinks on 14.c4 and 19.Ng3. With 55m 56s against Gukesh's 16m 18s, Sindarov could afford the time and still kept a big lead at 47m 20s.

likely_reasons.reason: The three good options were very different in kind, and g4 permanently changes the pawn structure, which probably called for careful thought.
The game was seven moves past known theory, so Sindarov likely had to work things out at the board.
A large clock lead meant Sindarov could spend time without much risk.

narrative.headline: Gukesh finds the only safe king move quickly
narrative.text: After Sindarov captured on h6 with check, Gukesh answered with 32...Kg8 in just 12 seconds, and the engine rates it as the best move, keeping the game level at 0.0. It was an only-move situation: with five legal king moves available, the engine saw just one good choice, while Kf6 and Kg6 would have dropped Gukesh to about -5.0 and -5.45. One likely reason for the speed is the clock, since Gukesh had only 5m 42s left against Sindarov's 17m 20s. Gukesh had already spent heavy time earlier, including a 36-minute think on 17...Bb4 and long thinks on 12...Be7 and 13...Bd7, so there was little left to spend. Sindarov had taken 1m 33s over the check, which may have given Gukesh time to see the retreat coming. The game was 19 moves past known theory, in a queenless middlegame where precise calculation mattered.

likely_reasons.reason: Gukesh was short on time, with 5m 42s against Sindarov's 17m 20s, so a fast reply was probably necessary.
Being in check with only five legal moves and just one good one, the choice may have been easier to narrow down than the engine's difficulty score suggests.
Sindarov spent 1m 33s on the checking capture Bxh6+, which may have given Gukesh time to prepare the king retreat in advance.

narrative.headline: Sindarov finds the only move in seconds
narrative.text: Sindarov played 38.Rh5 in just 12 seconds, and the engine rates it as the only good move in the position, holding the balance at 0.00. The alternatives were disastrous: the engine scores Bf8 at -5.75 and Rd5 at -6.5 for Sindarov. Despite the difficulty rating being at its maximum, Sindarov may have seen quickly that the rook had to go to h5, with the engine line continuing Kg8 Rg5+ Kh7. One likely reason for the speed is that Gukesh's previous move, 37...Kh7, was a quiet king move that probably left a natural follow-up. Sindarov had already spent heavily earlier, with long thinks on 14.c4, 19.Ng3 and 22.Ne1, but still held a comfortable clock lead of 15m 51s against Gukesh's 6m 38s. With 24 moves since leaving theory and few pieces left, the position may have become concrete enough to calculate fast.

likely_reasons.reason: Rh5 was the only move that kept the balance, and every alternative the engine checked lost heavily, which can make the right choice stand out.
Gukesh's quiet king move 37...Kh7 probably invited a direct rook reply, matching the engine line Rh5 Kg8 Rg5+ Kh7.
Sindarov's earlier long thinks may have prepared the ground, and a solid clock lead meant no time pressure forcing a rushed decision either way.
